title: Acts 12:1–25
context: King Herod kills James the brother of John and, seeing that this pleases the Jewish leaders, arrests Peter during the feast, while the church prays earnestly for him. On the night before his trial an angel wakes Peter, his chains fall off, and he walks out past the guards into the city. He goes to the house of Mary, mother of John Mark, where the servant girl Rhoda is so overjoyed that she leaves him knocking at the gate. Herod executes the guards; later, accepting praise as a god in Caesarea, he is struck by an angel and dies. The word of God continues to grow, and Barnabas and Saul return with John Mark.

verses.text: Now about that time, King Herod stretched out his hands to oppress some of the assembly.
verses.arminianNotes: Herod lays hands on some of the church to harm them. Arminian readers see political power turning against believers.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see rulers opposing Christ as Psalm 2 foretold.

verses.text: He killed James, the brother of John, with the sword.
verses.arminianNotes: He kills James, the brother of John, with the sword. Arminian commentators see that God does not always rescue his servants from death.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed commentators see God’s sovereign purposes in both James’s death and Peter’s rescue.

verses.text: When he saw that it pleased the Jews, he proceeded to seize Peter also. This was during the days of unleavened bread.
verses.arminianNotes: Seeing it pleases the Jews, he arrests Peter during Unleavened Bread. Arminian readers see a ruler seeking popularity.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the timing echoing Jesus’ arrest at Passover.

verses.text: When he had arrested him, he put him in prison and delivered him to four squads of four soldiers each to guard him, intending to bring him out to the people after the Passover.
verses.arminianNotes: He puts Peter under four squads of soldiers, planning a public trial after Passover. Arminian expositors see heavy security that only God could overcome.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed expositors see human precautions that cannot stop God.

verses.text: Peter therefore was kept in the prison, but constant prayer was made by the assembly to God for him.
verses.arminianNotes: Peter is kept in prison, but the church prays earnestly for him. Arminian readers see prayer as something God genuinely responds to.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see prayer as the means God ordained to accomplish his purpose.

verses.text: The same night when Herod was about to bring him out, Peter was sleeping between two soldiers, bound with two chains. Guards in front of the door kept the prison.
verses.arminianNotes: The night before his trial Peter sleeps between two soldiers. Arminian commentators see peace in danger.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed commentators see rest that comes from trusting God’s care.

verses.text: And behold, an angel of the Lord stood by him, and a light shone in the cell. He struck Peter on the side and woke him up, saying, “Stand up quickly!” His chains fell off his hands.
verses.arminianNotes: An angel strikes Peter’s side, wakes him, and the chains fall off. Arminian readers see God intervening dramatically.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see deliverance that is entirely God’s work.

verses.text: The angel said to him, “Get dressed and put on your sandals.” He did so. He said to him, “Put on your cloak and follow me.”
verses.arminianNotes: The angel tells him to dress and follow. Arminian expositors note that Peter must still get up and act.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed expositors see God directing every step.

verses.text: And he went out and followed him. He didn’t know that what was being done by the angel was real, but thought he saw a vision.
verses.arminianNotes: Peter follows, thinking he is seeing a vision. Arminian readers see that he does not grasp what is happening.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God working beyond his servant’s understanding.

verses.text: When they were past the first and the second guard, they came to the iron gate that leads into the city, which opened to them by itself. They went out and went down one street, and immediately the angel departed from him.
verses.arminianNotes: They pass the guards, the iron gate opens by itself, and the angel leaves. Arminian commentators see obstacles removed one by one.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed commentators see every barrier yielding to God’s will.

verses.text: When Peter had come to himself, he said, “Now I truly know that the Lord has sent out his angel and delivered me out of the hand of Herod, and from everything the Jewish people were expecting.”
verses.arminianNotes: Peter realizes the Lord sent his angel to rescue him. Arminian readers see understanding dawning after the event.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Peter acknowledging God’s providence.

verses.text: Thinking about that, he came to the house of Mary, the mother of John who was called Mark, where many were gathered together and were praying.
verses.arminianNotes: He goes to the house of Mary, where many are praying. Arminian expositors see the church still praying.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed expositors see the answer arriving while the prayer continues.

verses.text: When Peter knocked at the door of the gate, a servant girl named Rhoda came to answer.
verses.arminianNotes: Rhoda comes to answer the knock. Arminian readers note the vivid detail of an eyewitness account.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s care touching ordinary moments.

verses.text: When she recognized Peter’s voice, she didn’t open the gate for joy, but ran in and reported that Peter was standing in front of the gate.
verses.arminianNotes: Overjoyed, she runs back without opening. Arminian commentators see the humor of joy outrunning sense.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed commentators see the church slow to believe its own answered prayer.

verses.text: They said to her, “You are crazy!” But she insisted that it was so. They said, “It is his angel.”
verses.arminianNotes: They tell her she is out of her mind; then they say it is his angel. Arminian readers see weak faith even in praying believers.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God answering prayers offered with imperfect faith.

verses.text: But Peter continued knocking. When they had opened, they saw him and were amazed.
verses.arminianNotes: Peter keeps knocking, and they are amazed. Arminian expositors see persistence finally rewarded.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed expositors see God exceeding expectations.

verses.text: But he, beckoning to them with his hand to be silent, declared to them how the Lord had brought him out of the prison. He said, “Tell these things to James and to the brothers.” Then he departed and went to another place.
verses.arminianNotes: He tells how the Lord brought him out, sends word to James, and leaves. Arminian readers note James, the Lord’s brother, now leading.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Peter giving God the credit.

verses.text: Now as soon as it was day, there was no small stir among the soldiers about what had become of Peter.
verses.arminianNotes: At daybreak the soldiers are in turmoil. Arminian commentators see human plans thrown into confusion.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed commentators see God’s action confounding the powerful.

verses.text: When Herod had sought for him and didn’t find him, he examined the guards, then commanded that they should be put to death. He went down from Judea to Caesarea, and stayed there.
verses.arminianNotes: Herod examines the guards and executes them. Arminian readers see cruelty from a frustrated ruler.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the contrast between the tyrant and the God who rescues.

verses.text: Now Herod was very angry with the people of Tyre and Sidon. They came with one accord to him and, having made Blastus, the king’s personal aide, their friend, they asked for peace, because their country depended on the king’s country for food.
verses.arminianNotes: Herod is angry with Tyre and Sidon, who seek peace because they depend on his land for food. Arminian expositors see political maneuvering.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed expositors see the setting for Herod’s downfall.

verses.text: On an appointed day, Herod dressed himself in royal clothing, sat on the throne, and gave a speech to them.
verses.arminianNotes: Herod sits on his throne in royal robes and gives a speech. Arminian readers see pride on display.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see human glory set against God’s glory.

verses.text: The people shouted, “The voice of a god, and not of a man!”
verses.arminianNotes: The people shout, “The voice of a god, and not of a man!” Arminian commentators see flattery Herod accepts.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed commentators see a creature accepting worship due to God alone.

verses.text: Immediately an angel of the Lord struck him, because he didn’t give God the glory. Then he was eaten by worms and died.
verses.arminianNotes: An angel strikes him because he did not give God the glory, and he dies. Arminian readers see judgment on pride.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God defending his glory.

verses.text: But the word of God grew and multiplied.
verses.arminianNotes: But the word of God grows and multiplies. Arminian expositors see the gospel outliving its persecutor.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed expositors see the contrast between the dying king and the living word.

verses.text: Barnabas and Saul returned to Jerusalem when they had fulfilled their service, also taking with them John who was called Mark.
verses.arminianNotes: Barnabas and Saul return with John Mark. Arminian readers see the stage set for the first mission.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God gathering the team he will send.
